prize_parts.citation: For an oeuvre that renews poetry, the essay and verse narrative through a formally inventive dialogue between antiquity and modern experience, giving loss, desire and the limits of translation new literary form.

statement.case_for: My writer is unchanged: Anne Carson. My citation wording has changed, and I explain why below. The case rests on the writing and not on the shared opening ranking, which says nothing about merit. Her voice is recognisable within a few lines, with its dry syntax, sudden turns and exposed feeling. Autobiography of Red recasts the Geryon material as a verse novel in which love and self-recognition are carried by the form. Nox turns an elegy for her brother into a made object where translation, commentary, archive and grief cannot be separated. The same concerns recur across essays, verse, drama and versions from Greek: loss, desire, and how unreliable the inherited tradition is. That recurrence is what I mean by sustained quality here. It seems to me to be a single project that has changed what English-language poetry and the essay can do. From the chair's questions I draw two consequences for the citation. First, the credited core should be the original lyric, verse narrative, essay and elegiac work. Second, the citation should name the encounter between antiquity and modern experience, not a genre. My round-1 wording named poetry and the essay but left out narrative, and that left out Autobiography of Red, which is one of her two representative works. I have added it. All of this rests on public knowledge of representative works. I have not independently verified texts or the full corpus.
statement.case_against: The strongest reservation is still maturity. Individual books are often short or fragmentary, and I do not know the most recent decade well enough to say whether it deepens the project or refines a settled method. A second reservation is that part of the effect depends on typography, book design and Greek allusion, which are hard to judge in translation and from a citation alone. A third is that Carson is a poet-scholar, so part of her fame may rest on erudition and not on the poems themselves. If a close reading of the later books showed repetition, the balance would move toward Cărtărescu, and I would say so openly. I do not treat my own ignorance of the late work as evidence that it repeats. It is an uncertainty that counts neither for nor against her, and I will not turn it into a negative merely to look rigorous.

responses.point: Mattson proposes that if continuing invention in the later work cannot be established, that should count against Carson and be stated openly. She also says repeated reinvention of the book as a form is evidence of development and not only of a stable manner.
responses.response: I accept that the committee must state openly what it cannot establish, and I will not claim a late phase I do not know. I would separate two things, though. The first is evidence of repetition. The second is a gap in our knowledge. Only the first should count against her, and the second belongs in the uncertainties. Within that limit I agree with your reading of development. The move from the verse novel to the book-object elegy is a change of solution, not only a refinement. I accept that this inference is open to challenge by anyone who knows the recent books better than I do.

responses.point: Palm names the verse novel and the book-length elegy as the core where the formal reinvention is fullest. She treats Cărtărescu's late phase, Solenoid in particular, as evidence that his ambition keeps extending, and she flags repetition risk and sentence-level translation loss in his very long novels.
responses.response: I agree on the core, and I have changed my citation to match: it now names verse narrative as well as poetry and the essay. On Cărtărescu we agree on both the strength and the risk. Solenoid looks to me like a late book that expands his materials, and that is the best maturity argument for keeping him my first alternative. But the repetition risk in very long novels and the loss of sentence-level texture are real. I cannot test either from translation, and that is part of why I do not put him first. We differ on one point. You treat the fragment as part of Carson's method, and I agree, but I would not use that to avoid the burden of showing deepening. Compression is a strength only if each book finds something new.

responses.point: Swärd argues that sustained quality is not the same as volume, and that because Carson writes in English the committee can assess her directly. Cărtărescu's Romanian she cannot judge, so she weighs that uncertainty against him more heavily.
responses.response: I agree that volume is not quality, and that is why I do not use scale alone against Carson. On direct assessment I want to be careful. Being able to read a writer in the original is an advantage for the evidence, not a merit. The committee could end up preferring the candidate whose corpus it knows best. I would therefore use access only to decide how firmly to state a judgment, not to rank the writers. Mattson made the same point about every candidate on this list. Applied that way, Carson's strength still seems to me to come from the work. Her treatment of grief and desire in the original English is where I find it.

responses.point: Olsson asks colleagues who know the Greek and English texts best to say whether the poems work for a reader without the sources. He also says an agreed citation text matters more than a rank, because it fixes what is being credited.
responses.response: I cannot speak as a Greek specialist and will not pretend to. My judgment of the poems comes from public knowledge of the works, not from any claim to have checked the sources. On that basis, the Geryon story reads to me as a modern love narrative whose force does not depend on knowing the fragments. In Nox the elegy is carried by the brother's death. On the chair's question about Nox, I would not exclude it from the original writing. Translation there is the elegiac method, so a citation that puts translation aside would misdescribe the book. The wording I propose covers it through 'the limits of translation' as a subject. It does not credit her translations or her classical scholarship as such. I agree with you that fixing the citation text matters more than the order of preference.

uncertainties: Whether Carson's most recent books deepen or repeat the project. I know this period least well and have not independently verified it.
Where the line falls between original writing and translation or scholarship, particularly in Nox, where translation functions as method.
How far typography, page design and book-object form can be judged in a text-based assessment or in Swedish and other translations.
Whether the compressed and fragmentary scale of much of the work satisfies the criterion of sustained significance as well as large-scale cumulative work does.
For Cărtărescu, how much of the sentence-level texture of the Romanian prose and the poetry survives translation, and whether the long novels extend or repeat their motifs.
For Zurita, how to weigh the landscape and sky-writing works, known mainly through documentation, against the printed books, and how the Spanish diction holds in translation.
The coverage of translated corpora for every shortlisted writer is unknown to me. I have not verified any text.
statement.conflict_note: None apparent from the supplied profile that would require recusal, and my disclosure is unchanged. My own practice concerns Central Europe and Nazism-era history, I have lived in Prague and Vienna, and I am a critic at Dagens Nyheter. Cărtărescu, one of my two alternatives, is an Eastern and Central European writer. This is context only and does not establish a preference, and the profile records no tie to him or to Carson or any other shortlisted writer. I was elected alongside Ingrid Carlberg, which is a collegial tie and not a conflict. Carlberg's simulated vote is a modeling assumption.
